pages.title: Fancy Text Generator — 80+ Copy-Paste Styles, No Popups
pages.metaDescription: Turn plain text into bold, italic, cursive, small caps, bubble, strikethrough and 80+ more copy-paste Unicode styles. Updates as you type. No sign-up, no popups.

pages.intro: This is a fancy text generator that does the one thing you came here to do, then gets out of the way. You type on the left, it converts your letters into Unicode characters that look like other fonts — script, bold, double-struck, small caps, circled, and around eighty more — and you copy whichever one you like. That's it. No account, no "allow notifications", no four ad blocks stacked on a 40-pixel tool. It's all real text, so the result pastes anywhere: Instagram and TikTok bios, Discord, X, WhatsApp, game tags, your Notion headers, wherever. If a glyph shows up as a box in some app, that's the app's font being stingy — pick another style and move on. Pin the ones you use a lot; they'll sit at the top next time you visit.

pitfalls.title: Don't run a whole paragraph through it
pitfalls.text: Beyond a line or two it gets hard to read, and many screen readers announce these characters one at a time ("mathematical bold small a, mathematical bold small b…"). Short and intentional only.

pitfalls.title: Don't use it in real web content
pitfalls.text: Search engines and assistive tech see a string of math symbols, not styled text. For a web page, use actual HTML/CSS. For a bio with zero formatting options, this is the workaround.

pitfalls.title: Don't expect the @username to take it
pitfalls.text: Username fields are the strictest. If a username won't accept a style, the bio almost always will — and Bold (sans) is the universal fallback.

pitfalls.title: Don't panic when you see empty boxes
pitfalls.text: That's the receiving app missing a glyph, not corruption. Pick a more widely-supported style; Bold, Small Caps and Full-width box out the least.

faqs.q: Is this actually free?
faqs.a: Yes. There's one ad unit further down the page and that's the entire business model. No paywall, no "pro" tier, no email gate. Type, copy, leave.

faqs.q: What's the difference between this and a real font?
faqs.a: A real font is a file that changes how text is drawn. This swaps your letters for different Unicode characters that happen to look fancy — so the styling travels with the text wherever you paste it, even somewhere that has no idea what font you used.

faqs.q: Why do some styles break on certain apps?
faqs.a: Some apps restrict which Unicode ranges they'll display in fields like usernames or bios, and some fonts simply don't include a glyph for a given character — you'll see empty rectangles either way. Bold, Small Caps and Full-width are the most widely supported; start there if an app is being difficult.

faqs.q: Do you store what I type?
faqs.a: No. Everything runs in your browser. The text never leaves your device, and the only thing saved locally is which styles you've pinned and your light/dark choice.

faqs.q: Can I get those symbols ✦彡 around my name?
faqs.a: Those are separate symbol characters, not a restyling of your letters. Style your name with one of the rows here, then add a symbol on each side. One clean letter style plus one or two symbols looks far better than stacking effects.

faqs.q: Which style should I pick if I just want it to look good and work everywhere?
faqs.a: Bold (sans). It's the most reliably rendered of all of them, it stays legible, and it gets past more username filters than anything else. Small Caps is a solid second choice for a calmer look.

pages.title: Cursive Text Generator — Copy-Paste Script & Calligraphy Fonts
pages.metaDescription: Generate cursive, script and calligraphy-style text you can copy and paste anywhere. Bold script too. Updates as you type, no sign-up, no popups.
pages.lede: Type and the cursive version is right there on the right. Bold script and a couple of related looks in the dropdown.
pages.intro: If you want your name in flowing 𝓼𝓬𝓻𝓲𝓹𝓽 on an Instagram bio or a wedding-ish caption, this is the page. It maps your letters onto the Unicode "mathematical script" characters — the loopy ones — plus the bolder calligraphy variant for when the thin version disappears against a busy background, and the heavier blackletter option in the same dropdown if you want something more dramatic. A few honest notes from testing: Instagram and TikTok bios handle cursive fine; Discord renders it perfectly; X is fine in posts but trims it in display names sometimes; and a handful of keyboards on Android won't show the script glyphs at all, which isn't something this tool can fix — it's the device font. Cursive Unicode has no real numbers or symbols, so digits and punctuation stay plain.

where.intro: Cursive is one of the better-supported decorative styles, but it has two specific weak points: the @username field on social apps, and a few Android keyboards.

rows.note: Reliable in the bio and captions. The @username field rejects it on a lot of accounts — that's the strictest field Instagram has.
Fine. Username field is stricter, like Instagram.
Renders everywhere, including nicknames. One of the most reliable platforms for script.
Posts and bio fine. Display names can be trimmed; the @handle won't accept it at all.
Works. Rendering of the swashier letters varies a little by device font.
A few stock keyboards and older Androids draw the script glyphs as boxes. Nothing the tool can do — it's the system font. Bold script sometimes fares slightly better.
Many game name filters reject script characters. If it bounces, try Bold (sans) or Small Caps instead.

items.label: Instagram / TikTok bio name
items.text: A first name in 𝒿𝑜𝓇𝒹𝒶𝓃 reads as personal and intentional; pair it with a single symbol on each side rather than piling on more effects.

items.label: Caption flourish
items.text: One word — 𝓪𝓮𝓼𝓽𝓱𝓮𝓽𝓲𝓬, 𝓭𝓻𝓮𝓪𝓶𝔂, 𝓼𝓸𝓯𝓽 — at the start of a caption sets a tone without rewriting anything.

items.label: Display name on Discord
items.text: Discord renders script in nicknames cleanly, so a server name in cursive actually sticks (unlike on Instagram, where the username field fights you).

items.label: Group chat name
items.text: A short cursive title for a group reads softer than the default. Numbers will stay plain, so skip dates in the name.

items.label: Bold script for busy backgrounds
items.text: On a photo or a colorful banner, thin script can vanish. Switch to 𝓫𝓸𝓵𝓭 𝓼𝓬𝓻𝓲𝓹𝓽 in the dropdown — same flavor, more weight.

pitfalls.title: Don't try to put numbers in script
pitfalls.text: There's no script version of 0–9 in Unicode, so digits stay normal and the effect looks half-finished. Keep numbers out of cursive text, or accept that they'll be plain.

pitfalls.title: Don't expect it to work in your Instagram @username
pitfalls.text: That field rejects cursive on most accounts. Style the bio instead — it almost always takes it.

pitfalls.title: Don't use it for a logo or anything that gets printed
pitfalls.text: These are display characters meant for text fields, not a licensed typeface. For a logo or a tattoo stencil, get an actual script font file. As a mockup, fine.

pitfalls.title: Don't assume "calligraphy" means something different
pitfalls.text: "Calligraphy font generator" and "handwriting font generator" point to the same characters — there's the regular script set and the bold script set, that's it. The heavier blackletter look is the Old English page.

faqs.q: Will cursive text work in my Instagram bio?
faqs.a: Yes, in the bio and in captions. It can fail inside the @username field on some accounts — that field is the strictest one Instagram has. If the username won't take it, the bio almost always will.

faqs.q: Why do my numbers stay normal?
faqs.a: The Unicode script range only covers A–Z and a–z. There aren't script versions of 0–9 or most punctuation, so this tool leaves them as-is rather than faking it badly.

faqs.q: Cursive vs. calligraphy vs. handwriting font — what's the difference here?
faqs.a: For copy-paste purposes they're the same trick: there's the regular script set and the bold script set. "Calligraphy" and "handwriting" land on the same characters. The Old English page covers the heavier blackletter look.

faqs.q: Can I use this for a logo or print?
faqs.a: Not really — these are display characters meant for web text fields, not a licensed typeface. For a logo you want an actual font file. For a bio, caption, or username, this is exactly the right tool.

faqs.q: Why does cursive show as boxes on my friend's phone?
faqs.a: Their device's font is missing those glyphs — usually an older Android or a third-party keyboard. It's not broken on your end; their phone just can't draw those characters. Bold script or Small Caps sometimes render where thin script doesn't.

faqs.q: What's the difference between regular script and bold script?
faqs.a: Bold script (𝓫𝓸𝓵𝓭) has heavier strokes, so it holds up against busy backgrounds, colored banners and photos where the thin version (𝓈𝒸𝓇𝒾𝓅𝓉) gets lost. Pick it from the dropdown when the regular one looks faint.

pages.title: Bold Text Generator — Copy-Paste 𝗕𝗼𝗹𝗱 Font & Letters
pages.metaDescription: Make bold text you can copy and paste — into Instagram, Discord, X, LinkedIn, anywhere that won't normally let you bold things. Sans and serif bold. No popups.
pages.lede: Bold version on the right — sans and serif. Bold italic and bold script in the dropdown.
pages.intro: Most places that won't let you bold text — Instagram captions, your X bio, a LinkedIn post, a Discord message that doesn't take markdown — will happily display 𝗯𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝗨𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗼𝗱𝗲. That's what this does: it swaps your letters for the bold mathematical alphanumerics, in the clean sans flavor (𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀) and the chunkier serif one (𝐥𝐢𝐤𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬), with bold italic and bold script also in the dropdown. Bold sans is the safest of all the styles on this site — if any fancy text is going to render in an app, it's this one — which is why it's the first one to reach for when something is being picky. It does have numbers and basic digits, unlike most decorative styles. Worth knowing: this is for short bits, not paragraphs.

where.intro: Bold is the workhorse. It renders in more places than any other style here, but a couple of profile fields still strip it.

rows.note: Bold sans frequently survives even in the @username field — rare for a fancy style. Bio and captions always work.
Fine. Username field is stricter but bold sans is your best shot at it.
Works everywhere. Use Discord's own **markdown** inside messages; use this for nicknames, statuses and bots that ignore markdown.
All fine. The @handle is still plain-only.
Posts and the headline usually keep bold (sans more often than serif). Some other profile fields strip it — check after pasting.
Works. WhatsApp also has its own *bold* with asterisks in messages; this is for the places that one doesn't reach.
Bold sans is the style most likely to pass a game's name filter. If even bold bounces, the filter is rejecting non-ASCII entirely.

examples.intro: Bold is for emphasis, not body text. Where it does the job:

items.label: Section headers in a flat editor
items.text: 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗻𝗲 stands out in tools that don't show real headings in certain views — task lists, simple notes, some wikis.

items.label: The one word that matters in a post
items.text: Bolding a single key word — 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝗲, 𝗻𝗼𝘄, 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 — pulls the eye without rewriting the whole sentence.

items.label: Instagram username (yes, really)
items.text: Bold sans is the rare fancy style that often passes Instagram's @username filter. Worth a try before settling for plain.

items.label: Game / Discord name
items.text: Clean, legible at small sizes, and the most filter-friendly. 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿_𝟬𝟭 — digits work too.

items.label: Bold + italic together
items.text: Pick Bold italic from the dropdown for 𝙗𝙤𝙩𝙝 𝙖𝙩 𝙤𝙣𝙘𝙚, or bold script if you want bold and cursive in one.

pitfalls.title: Don't bold a whole paragraph
pitfalls.text: It's tiring to read and some screen readers announce each character individually. Bold a header, a name, or a word — not a block of text.

pitfalls.title: Don't confuse sans bold with serif bold
pitfalls.text: Sans bold (𝗯𝗼𝗹𝗱) is cleaner and renders more reliably across apps; serif bold (𝐛𝐨𝐥𝐝) is heavier and more old-fashioned. When in doubt, pick sans — it boxes out the least.

pitfalls.title: Don't use it on your website for emphasis
pitfalls.text: Search engines and screen readers see math characters, not bold text. Use real HTML <strong> there. This is for apps that give you no formatting at all.

pitfalls.title: Don't expect Discord markdown to work in a nickname
pitfalls.text: **this** works in messages, not in nicknames, statuses or many bots. That's exactly where a Unicode bold is useful — paste it in.

faqs.q: Does bold text work on LinkedIn?
faqs.a: In posts and the headline, usually yes. LinkedIn occasionally strips it from certain profile fields, so check after pasting. Bold sans survives more often than bold serif.

faqs.q: Sans-serif bold or serif bold — which should I pick?
faqs.a: Sans bold (𝗯𝗼𝗹𝗱) is cleaner and renders more reliably across apps. Serif bold (𝐛𝐨𝐥𝐝) is heavier and a bit more old-fashioned. When in doubt, sans.

faqs.q: Is this bad for accessibility?
faqs.a: For a word or a name, it's fine. For long passages it's a real problem — some screen readers announce each character individually, e.g. "mathematical bold small a, mathematical bold small b...". Keep it to short, intentional bits.

faqs.q: Can I bold and italicize at once?
faqs.a: Yes — the Bold italic style in the dropdown does both. There's also a bold script option if you want bold and cursive together.

faqs.q: Do numbers work in bold text?
faqs.a: Yes — bold has a full set of digits (𝟬–𝟵 for sans, 𝟎–𝟗 for serif), unlike script, italic and most decorative styles. So a bold username with numbers in it works.

faqs.q: Why is bold the "safest" style?
faqs.a: The bold mathematical alphanumerics are some of the most widely-implemented characters outside plain ASCII — almost every modern font includes them. If any fancy style is going to render in a given app, bold sans is the one. It's the fallback to try when everything else boxes out.

pages.title: Small Text Generator — Tiny Text, Small Font & Small Caps
pages.metaDescription: Generate small text — tiny letters, small caps and subscript, all copy-paste. Also called small font, little text or mini text. Works in bios, captions and usernames. No popups.
pages.lede: Pick the small look you want on the right: tiny (superscript), small caps, or subscript.
pages.intro: "Small text" usually means one of three things, and they're genuinely different, so all three sit in the dropdown. There's tiny text — the superscript characters, ⁻ ˡⁱᵏᵉ ᵗʰⁱˢ — which is the closest to actual mini-letters but has gaps (a few letters like q look off, and uppercase mostly doesn't exist). There's ꜱᴍᴀʟʟ ᴄᴀᴘꜱ, which are small uppercase shapes at lowercase height — much more readable, complete A–Z, and the one most people actually want for an aesthetic bio. And there's subscript, the little dropped characters, mainly useful for chemistry-ish or footnote vibes. None of these are an actual smaller font size — they're separate Unicode characters drawn small. If you wanted to literally shrink text, that's a CSS thing, and no copy-paste tool can do it.

where.intro: Small caps is the reliable member of the family — full alphabet, widely supported. The tiny superscript option looks great in theory but has missing letters that pop back to full size, which is its own weak spot regardless of platform.

rows.note: Small caps displays cleanly in bios and captions. Superscript works too but any unsupported letter jumps to normal size.
Same — small caps reads well, superscript is patchy by design.
All three render, including in nicknames. Small caps is the most legible at nickname size.
Fine. Display names accept small caps; the @handle stays plain.
Works. Subscript digits in formulas render well; subscript letters are very limited.
Small caps often passes name filters; superscript and subscript are hit-or-miss because of the missing-letter fallbacks.

items.label: Aesthetic Instagram bio
items.text: ꜱᴍᴀʟʟ ᴄᴀᴘꜱ — full alphabet, stays readable, no letters jumping to full size. This is the one most "small text bio" searches actually want.

items.label: Footnote marker in a comment
items.text: Superscript digits — ¹ ² ³ — work perfectly, so a comment with a footnote reference reads cleanly even where there's no real superscript option.

items.label: Chemistry-style notation
items.text: Subscript shines here: H₂O, CO₂, x₁. The digits all have subscript forms, so formulas come out right.

items.label: A quiet username
items.text: Small caps as a username reads understated rather than shouty, and it passes more name filters than the tiny-text option.

items.label: A whole word in tiny letters
items.text: You can run a word through superscript, but expect a letter or two (and any capitals) to stay full-size. For a clean small word, switch to small caps.

pitfalls.title: Don't assume tiny text has a full alphabet
pitfalls.text: Unicode never finished the superscript letters — several lowercase letters and most capitals don't exist, so they fall back to full size and ruin the effect. Small caps has the complete set; use it when consistency matters.

pitfalls.title: Don't expect it to actually shrink the font
pitfalls.text: These are separate characters that happen to be drawn small — not a font-size change. Nothing pasted as text can resize text; that's controlled by the app.

pitfalls.title: Don't mix superscript letters and numbers expecting both to look small
pitfalls.text: The digits all have superscript forms, but the letters don't. A mixed string can come out with tiny numbers and full-size letters. Small caps avoids the mismatch.

pitfalls.title: Don't use subscript for general 'small text'
pitfalls.text: Subscript only covers a handful of letters — it's built for chemical formulas and footnotes, not for styling a whole bio. Reach for small caps for that.

faqs.q: Which 'small text' should I use for an Instagram bio?
faqs.a: Small Caps. It's the only one with a full alphabet, it stays readable, and Instagram displays it reliably in bios and captions. The superscript tiny-text option has missing letters that fall back to normal size and break the effect.

faqs.q: Why are some letters in tiny text the wrong size?
faqs.a: Unicode never finished the superscript alphabet. Letters like q, and most capitals, simply don't have a superscript form, so they stay full-size. Small Caps doesn't have this problem.

faqs.q: Can I make my whole comment tiny?
faqs.a: You can run a sentence through it, yes — just expect it to be harder to read and for the odd character to pop back to normal size. For more than a few words, Small Caps is the comfortable choice.

faqs.q: Is this the same as a 'subscript generator'?
faqs.a: Subscript is one of the three options in the dropdown. If you specifically need ₐ ₑ ₒ-style dropped characters — H₂O, x₁ — pick Subscript.

faqs.q: Does small caps count as uppercase or lowercase?
faqs.a: Visually it's small uppercase letterforms sitting at lowercase height. Apps treat the characters as their own thing, so it usually passes fields that allow letters. It reads as a calmer, more typeset version of all-caps.

faqs.q: Why do superscript numbers work but superscript letters don't?
faqs.a: Unicode defined a complete set of superscript digits (used in math notation) but only a partial set of superscript letters. So ¹²³ is fine; a word may have gaps. Same story, worse, for subscript letters.

faqs.q: Is this a 'small font' generator?
faqs.a: Sort of — 'small font' is what most people type, but none of these actually shrink the font size (that's a CSS thing the app controls). What you get are real Unicode characters drawn small: small caps for a full, readable alphabet, tiny superscript letters, or subscript. For the look most 'small font' searches want, pick small caps.

faqs.q: Small text, tiny text, little text, mini text — what's the difference?
faqs.a: Mostly different names for the same idea: swapping your letters for smaller Unicode characters. Here that's three real options — small caps (ꜱᴍᴀʟʟ ᴄᴀᴘꜱ, full A–Z, the most readable), tiny/superscript letters (the smallest, but with gaps), and subscript. There's no separate 'mini font'; pick whichever fits.

pages.title: Zalgo Text Generator — Glitchy, Cursed, Creepy Text to Copy
pages.metaDescription: Generate zalgo / glitch / cursed text — the corrupted-looking style with stacked marks. Adjustable intensity, copy-paste ready. No sign-up, no popups.
pages.lede: Glitch text on the right — mild by default so it actually survives. Crank the input and watch it fall apart.
pages.intro: Zalgo text — also called glitch text, cursed text or corrupted text — is the look where letters seem to be falling apart, bleeding marks above and below themselves. The trick is real Unicode: every character gets a random pile of "combining diacritical marks" stacked on top, which the browser dutifully renders all at once. This page keeps it on the milder side because the heavy version is borderline unreadable and a lot of apps will either reject it or chew up other people's screens with it — there's a reason Discord truncates the worst of it. Two practical warnings up front: zalgo is sometimes flagged or auto-removed by moderation bots (it's a classic way to break chat layouts), and it genuinely hurts accessibility, so it's a "profile name for fun" thing, not a "send this in a support ticket" thing.

where.intro: Zalgo is the least portable style on the site by design — the whole point is overloading the renderer. Treat anything past "mild" as unreliable.

rows.note: Discord caps the number of combining marks per message to stop layout abuse. Mild zalgo comes through; heavy zalgo gets truncated or stripped.
Light zalgo usually shows; heavier versions render inconsistently and can get visually clipped. The @username field rejects it.
Light works in posts. Display name field tends to reject or flatten stacked marks.
Renders, but heavy zalgo can break line spacing differently on Android vs iOS.
Almost universally rejected by name filters — combining-mark spam is exactly what those filters block. Use Bold or Full-width for a game name.
Don't. It's unreadable to screen readers and looks broken. Plain text only.

examples.intro: Where mild zalgo fits — and it really is just "for the bit":

items.label: A spooky Discord nickname
items.text: A name with a light dusting of marks reads as "glitched" without breaking the member list. Keep the intensity low or Discord truncates it.

items.label: Halloween / horror-theme caption
items.text: One word of mild zalgo at the start of a caption sets the tone. Don't zalgo the whole sentence — nobody can read it.

items.label: "Glitched" stream overlay text
items.text: If you're pasting into overlay software, mild zalgo gives a corrupted-data vibe. Test it renders in your tool first; some text engines flatten the marks.

items.label: An edgy username (where allowed)
items.text: Some platforms tolerate light zalgo in names; most games don't. If a name keeps getting rejected, that's why — tone it down or switch styles.

items.label: A joke about something being "cursed"
items.text: Run the word "cursed" through it. It's a small, self-aware gag — not a vibe you want spread across a paragraph.

pitfalls.title: Don't go max intensity and expect it to survive
pitfalls.text: Discord truncates it, many fields reject it, and on a phone it can overlap the line above. The milder it is, the more places it actually works.

pitfalls.title: Don't use it where people need to read you
pitfalls.text: Screen readers can't parse it, and moderation bots may auto-remove it as spam. Profile name for fun, yes. Anything that matters, no.

pitfalls.title: Don't try to "de-zalgo" pasted text
pitfalls.text: Once it's pasted, the marks are part of the text and the original spacing is gone. The fix is to regenerate from your plain text at a lower intensity, or just retype it.

pitfalls.title: Don't expect a game to accept it
pitfalls.text: Name filters block combining-mark stacks specifically. If you want a glitchy-looking game name, that's not zalgo — try Full-width or a Bold style instead.

faqs.q: Why does Discord cut off my zalgo text?
faqs.a: Discord caps the number of combining marks it'll render per message to stop people breaking the chat. Heavy zalgo gets truncated or stripped. Use a lower intensity and it'll usually come through intact.

faqs.q: Will zalgo text get me banned somewhere?
faqs.a: Not normally, but some servers and games auto-remove it or treat it as spam because it can mess with layouts. If a name keeps getting rejected, that's why — tone it down.

faqs.q: Is 'glitch text' the same thing?
faqs.a: Mostly, yes — "glitch text", "cursed text" and "corrupted text" all describe the same combining-marks technique. Some sites also call upside-down or strikethrough "glitchy"; here zalgo is the one with stacked marks.

faqs.q: Can I undo it / clean it up?
faqs.a: Once it's pasted, the marks are part of the text. Easiest fix: regenerate from the original plain text at a lower intensity, or just retype it. There's no reliable one-click "de-zalgo" because the original spacing is gone.

faqs.q: Why does it look different on my friend's phone?
faqs.a: Combining marks are positioned by each device's font, so the same zalgo string overlaps the line above on some phones and looks tidy on others. Heavier zalgo amplifies that difference. There's no fix beyond using less of it.

faqs.q: Is there a 'safe' amount of zalgo?

faqs.q: Single underline or double — what's the use case?

faqs.q: Can I underline and bold at the same time?

faqs.q: Should I use this on my website?

faqs.q: Underline vs. strikethrough — they look like the same kind of effect?

faqs.q: Can I strike through bold text?

faqs.q: Why does strikethrough show oddly on some words with spaces?

pages.intro: Bubble text is the round, ⓑⓤⓑⓑⓛⓔ-ⓛⓞⓞⓚⓘⓝⓖ one — each letter sitting inside a little circle. This page gives you the standard outline circles, the filled "negative" version (🅑🅛🅐🅒🅚 circles with the letter knocked out), and a squared option for when you want corners instead. Two things to know going in. First, the circled set has both uppercase and lowercase, but the filled version is uppercase-only — lowercase letters in that style just fall back to the uppercase circle. Second, numbers behave: there's a circled 1–9 and a separate circled 0 (⓪), so digits work, unlike most fancy styles. It pastes wherever — Instagram, TikTok, Discord, X — and it's a popular one for usernames because the circled glyphs are common enough that a lot of name fields accept them.

where.intro: Circled letters are some of the more widely-implemented decorative characters, so bubble text shows up in more name fields than most styles. The catch is the filled version being uppercase-only.

faqs.a: Unicode only defined the filled (negative) circled letters for A–Z uppercase. There's no lowercase set, so this tool uses the uppercase circle for both. The outline bubble style does have lowercase, so use that if you need it.

faqs.q: Do numbers work in bubble text?
faqs.a: Yes — circled 1 through 9 exist, and there's a separate circled zero (⓪). So unlike script or italic, you can bubble a number too. The squared style is letters only, though.

faqs.q: Is bubble text good for a username?
faqs.a: Often, yes — circled letters are widely supported, so a lot of platforms accept them in name fields, including Instagram's @username field more often than not. If one doesn't, the bio will, and bold sans is the universal fallback.

faqs.q: Bubble letters vs. squared letters?
faqs.a: Bubble = each letter in a circle (Ⓐ). Squared = each letter in a box (🄰). Same idea, different shape. Both are in the dropdown — pick whichever fits the vibe. Circled has numbers; squared doesn't.

faqs.q: Why do some bubble letters look filled-in on my friend's phone?
faqs.a: Different fonts draw the circled characters differently — some render them as thin outlines, others a bit heavier. The filled (negative) style is a separate set entirely. If you specifically want the knocked-out look, pick the filled option (uppercase only).

faqs.q: Can I make a whole sentence in bubble letters?
faqs.a: Sure — it's just characters, so it pastes fine. It reads a little slower than plain text, so it's better for a name or a short line than a paragraph. Numbers and basic letters all have circled forms; most punctuation stays plain.

pages.intro: There are two things people mean by "mirror text" and they're genuinely different, so both are in the dropdown. "Reversed" simply puts your characters in backwards order — txet sdrawkcab — same letters, right way up, just last-to-first. That's what you want for a puzzle, a hidden message, or text that reads correctly in a mirror's reflection. "Upside down" actually rotates the letters 180° (ǝ for e, d for p, and so on) and reverses them too, so it reads inverted — that's the gag-bio one. Reversed text is dead simple and works literally everywhere because it's just your normal characters reordered. Upside down is a bit more fragile since not every letter has a flipped Unicode form, so a few fall back to themselves. If you tried one and it wasn't the effect you pictured, switch to the other — nine times out of ten that's the fix.

rows.note: Reversed is just your normal characters reordered, so anything that accepts text accepts it. No glyph can box out because there are no special glyphs.

pitfalls.text: Reversed = same letters, backwards order, right way up. Upside down = rotated 180° and reordered, reads inverted. People want one and grab the other constantly. Try both — the difference is obvious once you see it.

faqs.q: Reversed vs. mirrored vs. upside down — which is which?
faqs.a: Reversed: characters in backwards order, still upright (olleh). Upside down: rotated 180° and reversed, so it reads inverted. "Mirrored" usually means reversed — text that looks right in a mirror. Both are in the dropdown; try both.

faqs.q: Does reversed text work everywhere?
faqs.a: Yes — it's just your normal letters in a different order, so any app that accepts text accepts this. There are no special characters to box out. Upside down is the one that occasionally has letters fall back to normal because Unicode lacks a rotated form for them.

faqs.q: Can I use this to write a secret message?
faqs.a: Sort of — reversed text is trivially easy to read back (read right-to-left, or paste it into another reverser), so it's more 'fun puzzle' than 'real secret'. Good for a riddle, not for anything you actually need hidden.

faqs.q: Why does upside down text look half-broken?
faqs.a: Because the rotated alphabet isn't complete — some letters, especially capitals, don't have an upside-down Unicode character, so they stay as they are. It's a known limit, not a bug.

faqs.q: Will a reversed username get rejected?
faqs.a: Less often than fancier styles — reversed text is made of plain characters, so it usually passes name filters that block special glyphs. If the upside-down version bounces, switch to plain reversed.

faqs.q: Can I reverse text and keep it readable?
faqs.a: Reversed text is readable if you read it backwards or run it through a reverser — that's the point. If you want it to read normally but look styled, you don't want this page; you want one of the font-style pages like cursive or bold.

faqs.q: Full-width vs. wide-spaced — which looks better?
faqs.a: Full-width makes each letter physically wider, which gives the strongest vaporwave effect. Wide-spaced keeps normal letters and just adds gaps — subtler, and a touch more reliable in apps that handle full-width awkwardly. Try both side by side.

faqs.q: Why did my wide spaces disappear?

faqs.q: Can I use the aesthetic look in my game name?

faqs.q: Is 'vaporwave text' the same as 'aesthetic text'?
faqs.a: Effectively yes — both point to the full-width Latin characters (and sometimes wide-spaced text and small caps). "Vaporwave font", "aesthetic font", "wide text" all land here.

pitfalls.text: There's no fraktur version of 0–9 in Unicode, so digits stay plain and the effect looks unfinished. Keep numbers out, or accept they'll be plain.

pitfalls.title: Don't be alarmed if a capital looks like the wrong letter
pitfalls.text: Historic blackletter drew certain capitals — notably C and I — in shapes that look strange to modern eyes. That's faithful to the original alphabet, not a glitch. If a reader might get confused, bold fraktur is a bit clearer.

pitfalls.title: Don't use this for an actual tattoo or print job
pitfalls.text: These are Unicode display characters, not a real typeface — they won't scale or print like a font file. As a mockup to show the look, fine. For the real thing, get a licensed blackletter font.

pitfalls.title: Don't expect it in a username
pitfalls.text: Fraktur usually gets rejected in username fields. For a name, bold sans is the fallback that passes most filters.

faqs.q: Old English, gothic, blackletter, fraktur — are these all the same?
faqs.a: For copy-paste purposes, yes — they all point to the Unicode fraktur characters. "Old English font" is the search term most people use; "blackletter" and "fraktur" are the typographically correct names. Same letters either way.

faqs.q: Why don't numbers work in Old English text?
faqs.a: The Unicode fraktur range covers A–Z and a–z only. There's no fraktur set for 0–9 or most punctuation, so this tool leaves them as normal characters rather than substituting something that doesn't match.

faqs.q: Can I use this for a tattoo design?
faqs.a: As a mockup or to show your artist the vibe, sure. For the actual stencil you (or they) should use a proper blackletter font file — these Unicode characters aren't a real typeface and won't scale or print the way a font will.

faqs.q: Some capital letters look like the wrong letter — why?
faqs.a: Historic blackletter drew certain capitals — notably C, I, and a few others — in shapes that look strange to modern eyes. That's faithful to the original alphabet, not a glitch. If a reader might get confused, the bold fraktur version is a bit clearer.

faqs.q: Fraktur vs. bold fraktur — when do I switch?
faqs.a: Use bold fraktur (𝖋𝖗𝖆𝖐𝖙𝖚𝖗) when the thin version (𝔣𝔯𝔞𝔨𝔱𝔲𝔯) gets lost — against a photo, a colored banner, at small sizes. It's the same letterforms with more weight, so it stays legible where the regular one fades.

faqs.q: Will Old English text show up on everyone's phone?
faqs.a: Mostly. A few older Androids and stock keyboards don't include the fraktur glyphs and show boxes — that's their font, not your text. Bold fraktur renders in some places the thin one doesn't; bold sans is the universal fallback.

pages.lede: Superscript on the right, subscript and small caps in the dropdown — small caps being the readable fallback when letters go missing.
pages.intro: Superscript is the tiny raised text — ˡⁱᵏᵉ ᵗʰⁱˢ — and subscript is the tiny dropped version, ₗᵢₖₑ ₜₕᵢₛ. Both come from real Unicode characters, so they paste anywhere: a footnote marker in a comment, math-ish or chemistry-ish notation (H₂O, x², that sort of thing), or just a small-text aesthetic on a bio. The thing nobody tells you: Unicode never finished either alphabet. Superscript is missing a few lowercase letters (and most capitals) — they fall back to full size — and subscript is even patchier, covering only a handful of letters. So a word that's all lowercase letters Unicode happens to have will look great; one with the wrong letters or any capitals will look half-broken. If you want consistent small-looking text with a complete alphabet, small caps (also in the dropdown) is the better tool — it just doesn't sit above or below the line.

where.intro: Where superscript and subscript render isn't really the issue — they're just characters, and they show up almost everywhere. The catch is internal: the alphabets have holes, so whether your specific word looks right depends on which letters it uses.

pitfalls.title: Don't assume superscript has a full alphabet
pitfalls.text: It doesn't — several lowercase letters and most capitals have no superscript form, so they stay full size. Subscript is even more limited. For consistent small text, use small caps.

pitfalls.title: Don't expect it to actually shrink the font size
pitfalls.text: These are separate characters drawn small — not a size change. Nothing pasted as text can resize text; the app controls that.

pitfalls.title: Don't put capital letters in superscript and expect them small
pitfalls.text: Almost no capitals have superscript forms — they'll stay full size. If you need a small-looking capital, that's what small caps is for.

pitfalls.title: Don't use subscript for general 'small text'
pitfalls.text: Subscript covers only a handful of letters — it's built for chemical formulas and footnotes, not for styling a bio. Reach for small caps for that.

faqs.q: Why are some of my letters full-size in superscript?
faqs.a: Because Unicode doesn't have a superscript version of every letter — several lowercase letters and most capitals just don't exist in that range, so they stay normal size. Subscript is even more limited. There's no fix; it's the character set's gap.

faqs.q: Superscript vs. subscript vs. small caps — what should I use?
faqs.a: Superscript for raised tiny text (footnotes, exponents). Subscript for lowered tiny text (chemical formulas). Small caps when you want a full word to read small and clean with no missing letters — it's the most reliable of the three for general 'small text'.

faqs.q: Can I write H₂O or x² with this?
faqs.a: Yes — the digits all have superscript and subscript forms, so numbers in formulas work well. It's letters where the gaps appear, not numbers.

faqs.q: Does this work in an Instagram bio?
faqs.a: Yes, in bios and captions. Just expect any unsupported letters to pop back to full size, which can ruin the effect — for a clean look across a whole word, small caps is the safer pick.

faqs.q: Why do superscript digits work but superscript letters don't?
faqs.a: Unicode defined a complete set of superscript (and subscript) digits because they're needed for math and chemistry notation, but only a partial set of letters. So numbers in formulas are fine; a word may have gaps.

faqs.q: Is there a superscript capital A, B, C…?
faqs.a: Mostly no. A handful of capital-ish superscript letters exist, but the set is far from complete, so most uppercase letters fall back to full size. If you need small-looking capitals, small caps gives you the whole alphabet.
